description: Independent recomputation of implemented widgets by an external process, recorded after release. Release files are immutable once committed, so evidence about a release lives here and accrues as checks run. A fixture digest recorded in a result is over canonical JSON content rather than the file’s bytes, revised 2026-10-11 because byte identity is unsatisfiable in the browser the lab publishes to. A parity result establishes numerical agreement with a named external implementation under a stated criterion. It is not scientific certification, and it says nothing about whether a method is appropriate for a question.

lab.pinNote: The commit CI checks the lab out at: .github/workflows/pages.yml reads it with `jq -r .lab.commit widgets/parity.json`. So this pin, not the clone beside this repository, is what `validate:dive-deeper` verifies against on a clean runner -- and it must be advanced whenever a check lands in the lab, in the same push-then-pin order the worked examples use.

outcomes.agrees: Every case met the stated criterion.
outcomes.partial: Some cases met it and others did not; the measurement states which.
outcomes.diverges: The stated criterion was not met.
outcomes.unresolved: The comparison could not be made, for a reason the note gives.

entries.criterion: maximum separation below 0.001 m over the fixture points
entries.measured: maximum separation 6.70e-5 m over 9 points
entries.note: Recomputed from the declared PROJ definition rather than the source EPSG code, so the comparison tests what the widget says it did. Covers a projection change on one datum; no datum shift is exercised.
entries.diveDeeper: Dive deeper · what a projection is, and what the zone choice costs

entries.criterion: identical opened window, included-cell set and retained values, per case
entries.measured: Cell-centre: agrees, 0 of 132 cells differ and retained values are identical. All-touched at a pixel-aligned cutline: 2 cells differ, both beside the alignment. All-touched with a one-pixel margin: the window differs and 61 cells differ, where the reference models the margin as a 3x3 binary dilation, which is not this widget's rule.
entries.note: Recorded per case rather than as one verdict. The two residual all-touched cells are what remains after adopting GDAL's positive-area rule, down from 35; see docs/experiments/29-raster-edge-inclusion.md. The margin case is an unresolved comparison, not an established defect: the reference and the widget define the margin differently.

entries.criterion: relative difference at most 1e-9 against an independent expression of the declared spherical formula, over five boundaries including one with a hole
entries.measured: Implementation: relative difference at most 4.78e-14. Reported separately as method context, not as failures — against a geodesic area with great-circle edges on the same sphere, boxes differ by under 0.01 % and a mid-latitude triangle with oblique edges by 0.30 %; against WGS84 the declared spherical approximation runs +0.45 % at the equator to -0.56 % at 60 N, so its sign changes with latitude.
entries.note: Three questions kept apart: whether the widget computes the formula it declares, how far that formula is from a great-circle-edged geodesic area, and how far from an ellipsoidal one. Only the first is a criterion; the other two quantify the approximation the widget already discloses when it calls its result approximate.

entries.criterion: projected mean within 1e-3 m on both axes, returned position within 1e-3 m ground separation, and the input count unchanged
entries.measured: Easting exact, northing 9.31e-10 m, returned position 4.09e-10 m ground separation over 6 points.
entries.note: Establishes that proj4js and PROJ agree on this UTM transform and that the average is unweighted as declared. It establishes nothing about whether a mean centre is an appropriate summary: the fixture includes an outlier 25 km from the cluster, and both implementations are pulled by it identically.

entries.criterion: the same set of reached nodes exactly, every cost within 0.01 m, and every remaining budget within 0.01 m of the budget less the cost
entries.measured: reached sets identical over 738 junctions, 142 each with none reached by only one implementation; worst cost difference 5.000e-03 m and worst remaining-budget difference 5.000e-03 m
entries.note: Compared against the implementation the original case study used: Advanced-1 NB03 reaches its isochrones with nx.ego_graph. The 5 mm residual is exactly the half-step of the two decimal places Fieldwork publishes, so the only disagreement is its rounding. Both traversals run on the edge lengths the fixture states and neither measures a street, so a wrong network passes in both. Covers outbound travel from one origin on one network; inbound is unexercised. Re-run against 0.3.0 after that release added speedMPerMin and travelMode to each junction: the parity validator refused evidence covering 0.2.0 while 0.3.0 was current, and the change being additive was not grounds for carrying the old result forward.

entries.criterion: entered and partial segment counts exactly, Fieldwork's area between 85% and 100.5% of the rule rebuilt at 1 m steps, and symmetric difference at most 8% of it
entries.measured: street selection identical -- 283 entered and 38 cut part-way in both; area 161044 against 160785 square metres, 0.160% apart, with a symmetric difference of 0.163%
entries.note: Rewritten 2026-10-14 with the widget. The corridor is no longer a constant strip: the walk off the street at the end of a route is charged, so the buffer at any point is min(bufferM, the budget left there) and tapers to nothing at the frontier, and the route now starts at the site rather than at the junction it was snapped to. The reference rebuilds that rule at 1 m steps with the exact remaining budget, where Fieldwork cuts at 12.5 m and rounds the radius down into six steps, so this measures the discretisation. Fieldwork draws 0.16% MORE ground than the rule, not less -- rounding down removes ground, buffering each chunk separately gives its far end a round cap the rule does not, and here the second is larger -- so the approximation is not purely conservative. Covers the five minute band of one corridor, outbound. Both implementations trust the same street lengths and geometry, so a wrong network passes in both. The notebook beside it measures the corridor at 0.55x for a 10 m final walk and 1.35x at 60 m, against a 25 m figure the case study records no reason for.

entries.criterion: the same number of hull vertices, every vertex within 0.001 m of one in the reference hull and vice versa, planar area within 0.05 m2, span within 0.1 m, and the located-point count unchanged
entries.measured: 11 hull vertices on both sides, worst vertex separation 1.95e-09 m, area difference 0.004 m2, span difference 0.018 m, over 250 located points
entries.note: A convex hull is exact, so there is no approximation to allow for and a disagreement would be real. The reference projects the points itself with pyproj rather than using Fieldwork's projected metres, so the projection and the hull are checked together. The area compared is the planar area of the ring in EPSG:32630, which is what the widget claims, and not a geodesic area. Agreement says nothing about whether a convex hull is a sensible summary: it fills in ground the outbreak did not cross, and both implementations fill it in identically.
entries.diveDeeper: Dive deeper · the assumption is the projection

entries.criterion: the same number of gaps filled, no interior ring left in the output, the filled geometry within 0.05 m2 by symmetric difference, and the areas before, after and added each within 0.05 m2
entries.measured: 69 interior rings dropped on both sides, zero rings left, symmetric difference 0.0e+00 m2, and the areas before, after and added agreeing to 3.5e-03 m2. The fill added 37293 m2 of 938166 m2
entries.note: Dropping interior rings is exact, so this checks the bookkeeping rather than a tolerance: the gap count, the area net of holes before, the outer rings after, and the difference. Two bands are used because the example has one pump, and a one-part fixture could not distinguish filling from joining up. Agreement says nothing about whether filling is right: the added ground was never computed as reachable, and the reference asserts it identically because it is the same operation.
entries.diveDeeper: Dive deeper · what the fill claims

entries.criterion: the combined geometry within 1 m2 by symmetric difference, the combined area and the summed parts area each within 1 m2, and the part and piece counts unchanged
entries.measured: combined area 701662.61 m2 against 701662.61 m2, a difference of 3.4e-03 m2, with a zero symmetric difference and the summed parts agreeing to 1.4e-03 m2 over 3 nested parts whose overlap is 240717 m2
entries.note: The most independent check in the lab so far: Fieldwork unions with polyclip-ts and measures with a shoelace sum, the reference unions with GEOS and measures with GEOS. A union is where two libraries most plausibly differ. The parts are three nested bands, so they overlap heavily and the union is not trivially the sum. Parts are summed net of their holes, which is the defect Fieldwork's own comment records finding on the isochrone chain: summing outer rings alone reported a hole-bearing area as overlapping itself.
entries.diveDeeper: Dive deeper · the sum is not the area

entries.criterion: the same polygons surviving the clip, each within 1e-13 square degrees of shapely's intersection by symmetric difference, and no output polygon extending beyond the boundary
entries.measured: all 8 of 8 polygons survived on both sides, worst symmetric difference 5.8e-18 square degrees, and none escaped the boundary
entries.note: polyclip-ts against GEOS on the John Snow chain: nearest-pump cells clipped to the reporting rectangle, which extend past it, so the clip does real work. Compared in square degrees because the widget intersects on longitude and latitude without projecting, which is declared rather than hidden. The notebook measures the cost of that: clipping in degrees and clipping in metres agree to 5.9e-5 relative at worst over a rectangle 1.4 km across -- 59 parts per million, about 6 m2 of 100,000 -- and the simplification would not hold for a continental boundary.
entries.diveDeeper: Dive deeper · the assumption is that degrees will do

entries.criterion: every per-polygon count, numeric total and missing-value count exact, and the summary of records, matched, unmatched, unlocated and multiply-assigned locations exact, with boundary policy 'include' read as GEOS covers
entries.measured: every per-polygon count and total exact over 250 locations in 8 polygons, summary exact, worst total difference 0
entries.note: Fieldwork's own point-in-polygon test against GEOS predicates, with the boundary policy mapped explicitly: include is covers, exclude is contains. The fixture contains no location on a polygon edge and none in two polygons, so that mapping is declared and NOT exercised by the comparison -- the notebook constructs the missing case to show that include counts an edge location for both cells and exclude for neither. Agreement says nothing about whether nearest-pump assignment models which pump anybody drank from.
entries.diveDeeper: Dive deeper · why the per-polygon totals must not be added

entries.criterion: each cell within 1 m2 of GEOS's Voronoi region for the same site by symmetric difference, the cells tiling the recomputed envelope to within 1 m2 with no overlap, and every cell containing its own site
entries.measured: all 8 cells within 2.5e-06 m2 of GEOS's region for the same site, union against the recomputed envelope 2.1e-06 m2, pairwise overlap 6.0e-07 m2, every cell holding its own site
entries.note: Two unrelated algorithms for the same partition: Fieldwork clips a rectangle with one half-plane per other site, the reference asks GEOS for the Voronoi diagram of the same projected points. Neither method informs the other. The envelope is recomputed from the boundary by the declared rule rather than taken from the fixture, so that derivation is checked too. This completes the John Snow Voronoi chain: cells, clip and count are all now independently recomputed. Agreement says nothing about whether a nearest-pump cell models which pump anybody drank from -- the notebook measures that 138,081 m2 of the ground reachable on foot in five minutes falls outside the cell, and the two answer different questions.
entries.diveDeeper: Dive deeper · the assumption is straight-line distance

entries.criterion: the order of identifiers exactly as the declared extent rule gives it, the same multiset of identifiers in and out, and the layer, polygon and banded-polygon counts exact
entries.measured: the order of all 3 identifiers exact, the same polygons in and out, the layer, polygon and banded counts exact, and 0 ties in extent
entries.note: A check of a rule rather than of arithmetic: this widget concatenates layers and sorts by extent, and has no geometry to compare. Extent is deliberately crude and is declared in full -- the sum of every ring's absolute shoelace area in SQUARE DEGREES, unprojected, holes added not subtracted -- because it is a sort key and not a measurement. The notebook measures the gap on the real bands: extent exceeds the net area by 0.6%, 10.8% and 7.6% for the 2, 5 and 10 minute corridors. Ties are reported because a tie would leave the order ambiguous while this check still passed; there are none here.
entries.diveDeeper: Dive deeper · why extent is the wrong number to quote

entries.criterion: exactly 128 vertices, the reported circle-area fraction within 5e-05 of the closed form for an inscribed polygon, and every vertex within 0.001 m of the stated 500 m on the sphere of radius 6.37101e+06 m that Turf buffers on
entries.measured: 128 vertices as expected, reported circle-area fraction 0.9996 against the closed form 0.99960, every vertex within 2.4e-09 m of the stated 500 m on Turf's sphere, and 500.28 to 501.59 m on the WGS84 ellipsoid
entries.note: Checked against theory rather than a second implementation: Turf buffers in a local azimuthal equidistant projection, so there is nothing equivalent to compare the construction with. A circle buffered with n/4 segments per quadrant is a polygon of n vertices inscribed in it, whose area is (n/2pi) sin(2pi/n) of the circle's -- arithmetic that owes nothing to any geometry library, and which reproduces the 0.99359 and 0.99960 this project measured by hand. This check FAILED on its first run at 1.589 m against a 1 m radius criterion, and the fault was the criterion. Turf buffers on a sphere of radius 6,371,008.8 m and does so exactly: the measured spread of vertex distances there is 0.0000 m. On the WGS84 ellipsoid the same ring is 500.28 to 501.59 m from the centre. So a 500 m buffer is 500 m on a sphere and up to 1.59 m more on the ground, varying with direction -- 0.32%, about 16 m on a 5 km scope. Nothing recorded that before, and it was found only because a criterion fixed in advance failed and was investigated instead of relaxed.
entries.diveDeeper: Dive deeper · what the step count buys

entries.criterion: the buffered area within 0.5% of a EPSG:32630 reference buffer at the same 8 segments per quadrant, and the result containing the original boundary
entries.measured: 12248049 m2 against 12235014 m2 from a EPSG:32630 buffer at the same 8 segments per quadrant, a relative difference of 1.1e-03, and the result contains the original boundary
entries.note: Exact agreement is not available and is not claimed: Turf buffers in a local azimuthal equidistant projection and the reference buffers in UTM, so the criterion is a relative area difference with the quadrant count declared. 8 segments per quadrant leaves 0.64% of an ideal circle outside the polygon against 0.04% at the 32 buffer_point uses, which is deliberate: this widget expands a boundary that already exists, so its edge decides nothing, while buffer_point's edge decides membership. The notebook measures where the approximation can even apply -- the corners are 13.4% of what this buffer adds and the sides are the rest, so the polygon approximation costs 0.086% of the addition.
entries.diveDeeper: Dive deeper · the buffer only matters at the corners

entries.criterion: the same node chosen for every site, the distance moved within 0.005 m -- half of the centimetre the widget reports it to -- the returned position being the node's and not the site's, the site and distinct-node counts exact, and no site beyond the 150 m limit
entries.measured: the same node chosen for all 8 sites against 738 nodes, worst distance error 3.7e-03 m against a reported precision of 0.01 m, every returned position being the node's, 0 equidistant ties, smallest margin to the second-nearest node 0.43 m
entries.note: A nearest-neighbour search and a distance, both exact. Eight pumps rather than the isochrone example's one, because a search over a single site exercises almost nothing. The criterion is 5 mm rather than 1 mm, and the reason is worth stating: the widget reports snapDistanceM as Number(d.toFixed(2)), so it computes in full precision and publishes centimetres, and 5 mm is half of its last reported digit rather than a statement about its accuracy. The first version of this check asked for 1 mm and failed at 3.7 mm, which was rounding and nothing else. The margin to the second-nearest node is reported because one site's is 0.43 m: no tie, so the answer is unambiguous, but the choice is decided by less than a pavement's width and a different datum would flip it. Agreement says nothing about whether snapping is harmless -- it moves the pumps 2.2 to 20.9 m, up to 5.6% of the five-minute band budget, and both implementations move them identically.
entries.diveDeeper: Dive deeper · snapping moves the site

external: none: a band is a threshold on distances the junctions carry
entries.criterion: the band budget within 0.005 m of minutes x the speed carried on the junctions, the same junctions selected, every remaining budget recomputed against the band to within 0.005 m, the counts exact, every kept junction stamped with the band, and the band nested rather than a ring
entries.measured: 142 of 706 junctions selected, band budget 375.00 m against 375.00 m recomputed from the speed on the junctions, worst remaining-budget error 5.7e-14 m, nested rather than a ring
entries.note: The arithmetic is a threshold and is not what this check is for. The design claim is that the widget restates neither the speed nor the direction, reading both from the junctions, so a band cannot disagree with the traversal that produced it -- and the reference tests exactly that, recomputing the budget from the speed carried on the junctions rather than from a parameter of its own. It also checks the part most likely to be got wrong: a junction's remaining budget is recomputed against the band, not carried over from the traversal. Here the traversal was 1,125 m and the band 375 m, so carrying it over would put fifteen minutes of reach at the edge of a five-minute corridor. The notebook measures the sensitivity to the walking speed, which is an estimate from photographs of 1854 London rather than a measurement: at 50 m/min 69 junctions are in the band, at 75 m/min 142, at 100 m/min 246. Walking 20% slower keeps about two thirds; a third slower halves it.
entries.diveDeeper: Dive deeper · the assumption is the walking speed

entries.criterion: per resolution: the same cells kept, the same count in each, each boundary and centre within 1e-09 degrees of h3-py's, the cells ordered by H3 index, and the matched and dropped point counts exact
entries.measured: at resolution 9, 5 cells kept and nothing dropped; at resolution 11, 52 cells kept, 13 withheld and 13 of 250 deaths removed from the output; cells, counts and order exact and every boundary and centre within 3.6e-14 degrees
entries.note: WEAKER THAN IT LOOKS, and the check says so: Fieldwork indexes with h3-js and the reference with h3-py, two bindings of the same C library, so the indexing is not independently verified. What is verified is that Fieldwork calls it correctly, orders by H3 index as declared, and applies its own sparse-cell rule. Two resolutions are used because the example's own setting does not exercise that rule: at resolution 9 all 250 deaths fall into five cells above the minimum and nothing is dropped, so resolution 11 is included to reach the case where points vanish. Agreement says nothing about whether aggregating to cells protects anybody; occupancy is not an anonymity guarantee, and at resolution 11 the rule silently removes 13 deaths rather than disclosing them.
entries.diveDeeper: Dive deeper · choosing the resolution, and for what

entries.criterion: per period: every bin key in order exactly, every weighted count exactly, the total exactly, every period between the first and last present including empty ones, and the dated and undated record counts exact
entries.measured: over 43 rows of Snow 1855 Table 1, all three periods exact: 43 day bins (12 with no deaths), 7 week bins, 2 month bins, every key in order, every weighted count and all three totals of 616
entries.note: Genuinely independent: Fieldwork bins with its own calendar arithmetic and pandas with resample, a different implementation of a different design, sharing no code -- unlike check 21 next door where both sides call the same C library. The week mapping was wrong on the first attempt, which is worth recording because the check's own docstring had already named the week as the dangerous case. Fieldwork keys a week by the Monday of its ISO week; the check used W-SUN with a left label, whose label is the preceding Sunday, so every key came out a day early while every count stayed plausible -- 7 bins, total 616, the peak in the right week. Only comparing the keys caught it. The correct mapping is W-MON with label and closed both left, and it is now spelled out rather than left implicit in a frequency string. Agreement says nothing about whether a curve by date of death says what a reader will take it to say: the shape by date of onset would be shifted earlier, and nobody recorded onset dates.
entries.diveDeeper: Dive deeper · what the period choice does to the curve

external: none -- a Python decision table derived from each ruleset's description, and a local N3 subset reader; no RDF library and no Fieldwork code
entries.criterion: two separate claims over the complete input space of each ruleset, 46 cells in all: every conclusion of the real EYE reasoner reproduced by a decision table written in Python from the ruleset's prose description, and the emitted receipt parsed and checked -- every asserted predicate declared by the input contract and no others, nine decimals on every bound number, one subject per cell, no dataset instance named in a rule, no unbound placeholder, and only math: builtins
entries.measured: exhaustive, not sampled. 12 cells for outreach-criteria, 10 for access-review, 24 for nb06-evidence -- the complete space of each. All 46 agree on conclusions and on receipt. 0 cells with no rule firing, 0 with two conclusions for one predicate. 19 rules in total across the three rulesets, using exactly two builtins, math:greaterThan and math:notGreaterThan, with no negation, recursion or aggregation anywhere. The boundary cell where the value equals the threshold is included in each table, which is what separates math:notGreaterThan from math:lessThan and what a sample would miss.
entries.note: The exemption this replaces said the decision is the reasoner's, which was a claim that no independent check was possible. Each ruleset's input space is finite, so the lab enumerates it completely. Two claims are recorded separately because they fail differently: a right answer nobody can audit, against a well-formed receipt for the wrong conclusion. Neither claim says any threshold is right; one ruleset claims a published basis and none of the three carries evidence a reader can open.
entries.diveDeeper: Dive deeper · the subset is the safety argument

entries.note: The widget that now hosts all three rulesets. The three entries beside this one cover policy, access_policy and xpert at the releases they were retired at, which is why they remain: parity covers a release, and those releases ran. This entry covers the host, and the check is the same check because the rulesets are the same rulesets -- the assembled rule text was proved byte-identical when they became data.

entries.criterion: maximum separation below 0.001 m over the fixture points, and the declared EPSG code names the same frame as the declared PROJ definition
entries.measured: maximum separation 0.000623 m over 9 points; declared code matches the declared definition
entries.note: The FORWARD direction, which release 0.2.0 performs. Check 01 covers the inverse that 0.1.0 did, so until this ran the widget's only evidence described a contract it no longer had and the catalog reported "agrees - earlier release". A round trip through both of Fieldwork's own directions is not a substitute: they come from one proj4 build, so a fault in its UTM would round-trip perfectly. The residual is the storage precision rather than the projection -- coordinates are kept to three decimals, whose combined rounding bound is 0.00071 m, and the worst separation is below it. The criterion's second clause exists because the proj4 string and the EPSG:326xx label are built separately from the zone: mutating the fixture's code from 32630 to 32631 leaves every coordinate agreeing to the same 0.62 mm and is caught only by comparing the frames.

entries.criterion: hull ring vertex for vertex within 1e-06 degrees, area within 0.01%, and the same status for the same stated comparison
entries.measured: the same 11-vertex hull ring vertex for vertex; area 139230.0 against 139230.0 square metres (0.0000%); and NoFlag from both, for the same stated comparison
entries.note: Covers a rule over a quantity DERIVED from geometry rather than over an imported column, which is what experiment 113 doubted was possible. The reference rebuilds the whole chain -- hull, area, threshold -- so a disagreement in the status would be as likely to be about the area as about the rule. The explanation is read for the same two numbers, so a status that agreed by accident would fail. It does not check the reasoner: the fixture records what EYE concluded and the reference recomputes the comparison in Python, which is check 23's job. Nor does it establish that 250,000 m2 is the right threshold, or a convex hull the right outline; the notebook beside it classifies the same observed outbreak as Review at 0.139 km2 and NoFlag at 0.250, against a figure the case study records no reason for.

entries.criterion: hull ring vertex for vertex within 1e-06 degrees, area within 0.01%, and the same status for the same stated comparison
entries.measured: the same 11-vertex hull ring vertex for vertex; area 139230.0 against 139230.0 square metres (0.0000%); and NoFlag from both, for the same stated comparison
entries.note: The same check, listed here because the first of its three leaps is this widget's: the area a hull derives has to be a FIELD on the polygon rather than a line in the run receipt, or no rule downstream can read it. Until 2026-10-14 it was computed, published as fw:hullAreaSquareMetres, and dropped. The hull geometry itself is checked by 10-hull.

entries.criterion: name similarity within 1e-9 of rapidfuzz; normalised names exact in both modes; distances within 1% of a WGS84 geodesic; blocked and compared counts exact; each pair's two agreements, score and class exact; and the merged count, output record set and every mergedFrom exact
entries.measured: The pipeline agrees in full: 16 pairs compared and 26 never compared, every normalised name, the two agreements, score and class of every pair, 3 merges with 2 matched pairs refused by the one-record-per-source rule, and all 11 output records with every mergedFrom. Distances agree to within 0.497% of a WGS84 geodesic against a 1% tolerance. One name comparison of seven diverges: abcvwxyz/cabvwxyz is 0.9375 here and 0.958333 in both references, a difference of 0.020833.
entries.note: Four independent recomputations, none sharing code with the widget: rapidfuzz and jellyfish for the name comparison, plain Python for the normalisation, a pyproj geodesic for the distances where the widget measures a great circle, and the blocking, scoring, classification and clustering reimplemented from declaredParameters alone. THE DIVERGENCE IS A CONVENTION, NOT A SLIP. Jaro halves the count of matched characters that are in a different order; this widget halves it exactly and both references halve it with integer division. Two independent references agreeing with each other is what settles that. It can only arise when the raw count is odd, which needs a cycle of odd length among the matched characters, and every published reference pair has an even count -- martha/marhta and dwayne/duane agree to six decimals here -- so no published value can detect it. No name pair in the fixture's two layers reaches it, which is why the pipeline agrees while this one constructed case does not. The records are constructed rather than downloaded so that every branch fires once: both comparisons agreeing, each agreeing alone, neither agreeing, a pair blocking never offered, a missing name, a record with no location, a same-source pair, and the cluster rule refusing a second record from one source. It says nothing about what the thresholds should be, which needs records whose true identity is known. It also surfaced a finding about the rule rather than the code: pairs are accepted in distance order, so a record named Annex sitting 2 m from another source's record for the main hospital takes that record, and the pair a reader would choose is then refused. Both implementations do it, because both follow the declared rule.

entries.criterion: the ratio within 1e-9 and both interval bounds within 1e-6 of statsmodels.stats.rates.confint_poisson_2indep(method='wald-log'), which is the same estimator by other authors -- a rate ratio is not a risk ratio and comparing against the wrong one would have agreed about nothing; the hard-coded z quantile against scipy.stats.norm.ppf; and the ratio recomputed from raw counts so a multiplier leaking into a dimensionless quantity would show as disagreement. Four comparisons over Snow's figures, per house and per person.
notEstablished: That the comparison is fair: no interval speaks to confounding, and these customers were not randomised.

That the log-normal interval is adequate at small counts. The Lambeth-only group has 18 events; a score interval is reported beside it rather than asserted equal. An exact conditional interval would be the better comparison and statsmodels documents that method as not yet implemented.
What the right denominator is. Houses and people give different ratios over the same outbreak, and choosing between them is the practitioner's.
entries.measured: Four comparisons agree in full. Snow's per-house ratio 8.4019 with a 95% interval of 6.8410 to 10.3189, against statsmodels at the same estimator; the per-person ratio 5.3511 (3.3549 to 8.5349) from the declared supply groups; the intermingled area 2.3090 (1.4456 to 3.6881) and 2.3175 (2.0924 to 2.5668) against Lambeth only and against the intermingled area. Ratios to within 1e-9 and both bounds to within 1e-6. The score method is reported beside each -- 6.8434 to 10.3152 on the first -- and never asserted equal, so what the declared approximation costs is visible rather than hidden.
entries.note: The intervals missed by more than 1e-6 on every comparison while the ratios agreed exactly -- the signature of a rounded constant rather than a wrong formula. Fieldwork hard-coded z as 1.9600 where the quantile is 1.959963984540054, moving Snow's per-house lower bound from 6.8409 to 6.8410. Immaterial at two decimals, and exactly the kind of thing an independent check exists to find before a reader does. Fixed in the same commit; the fixture was regenerated and all four agree.

entries.criterion: Eight cases, each recomputed from the fixture's three input tables and its own request with a pandas left merge on the FOLDED key -- the declared comparison reimplemented in the lab from its stated rule and never imported, because the folding is the thing under check. Compared as an ordered set of records so row order is not mistaken for disagreement: the produced rows, the row count, related, dropped and kept, the distinct brought categories in first-seen order, every unmatched key named with its count, the number of keys matched, and the retained share of each numeric variable summed independently. Two cases expect a REFUSAL and record what a merge does instead: an ambiguous key, where a merge returns 66 rows for a 64-row left table; and an undeclared gap, where a merge proceeds and leaves NaN. And the identity: a rate of one variable over another computed on the matched rows equals its value over every offered row multiplied by the ratio of their retained shares.
notEstablished: That exact matching is the right matching. Snow's two tables spell every sub-district identically, so this data never exercises a name that differs by punctuation or case -- the case a practitioner will actually meet. Fieldwork folds surrounding whitespace and nothing else, by decision rather than by this result.
That relating is right for bringing MEASURES across. That adds rows rather than a column and is deliberately not built, so nothing here speaks to it.

That the category is the right stratifier. Snow's third group -- sub-districts supplied by both companies -- is 300,149 of the 486,936 people in the table, and what to do with it is the practitioner's judgement, not an outcome of the join.
entries.measured: Three cases. The relate the example runs: 64 rows in, 64 out, 0 dropped, three categories in order, identical to the merge record for record. One sub-district withheld: 62 related, 2 dropped, the gap reported as {"St. Saviour, Southwark": 2 rows} and the same two rows a merge drops. An ambiguous key, constructed: refused with both company names in the message, where the same input through a merge returns 66 rows for a 64-row left table.
entries.note: Rebuilt 2026-10-28 for 0.3.0, and the regeneration MOVED NO COMPARED NUMBER on Snow's own two tables: they match 32 of 32 under either comparison, so the folded default leaves the example's figures exactly where they were. What changed is what the fixture can now reach. Check 28 had recorded, under what it could not establish, that "'St. George, Camberwell' against 'St George Camberwell' is the case a practitioner will actually meet, and neither this fixture nor this check reaches it" -- so the fixture now carries the published sub-district boundary as a second source for the same 32 names, which spells nine of them without their comma. The same two tables match 23 of 32 compared exactly and 32 of 32 compared folded: one knob, eighteen rows, and two retained shares that differ (68.24% of population against 61.16% of deaths). The lab confirms the identity that follows independently -- 3.109 x 0.8963 = 2.787 per 1000, observed 2.787 -- which is the arithmetic Fieldwork states and had not been checked from outside. Found on the way: 0.3.0 had BROKEN the fixture export outright, because two of the three old cases withhold or corrupt a key and the widget now refuses an undeclared gap. No gate runs export-validation-fixture.mjs, so nothing caught it.

entries.criterion: all six totals of the Snow contingency table exactly equal to pandas groupby(['water_supply','measure']).sum() -- integers, so the tolerance is zero rather than small -- with 6 groups from 64 rows and sub_district reported as the dropped column; and, with one cell emptied, that group null, equal to a per-group sum(skipna=False), the other five unchanged, and the gap naming the group with the rows summed and the rows empty adding to its row count. The size of the disagreement with the default sum is recorded in people rather than asserted.
notEstablished: That summing is right for these columns. It is right for counts and wrong for rates, and neither implementation can tell which it has been given. Fieldwork offers sum and nothing else for that reason; the protection is the absence of the other option, which no check can verify.
That nothing known is the right answer rather than the honest one. It refuses to guess; a practitioner who needs the number still has to find the missing cell.
That the three supply categories are the right strata. The both-companies group is 300,149 of 486,936 people, and what to do with it is the practitioner's judgement.
entries.measured: Six totals exact: 167,654 and 844 for Southwark and Vauxhall only, 300,149 and 652 for both companies, 19,133 and 18 for Lambeth only. With St. Saviour's population emptied, that group returns nothing known, matching a per-group sum(skipna=False); a default sum returns 147,945, short by 19,709 people. The gap is reported as 11 rows summed and 1 empty against the group's 12 rows.
entries.note: PANDAS HAS NO OPTION FOR THIS RULE, which the check found by reaching for the obvious one and watching it not work. `min_count=1` reads as "at least one value required" and is the first thing anyone writes here; it bounds how many values must be PRESENT rather than noticing any that are ABSENT, so on eleven numbers and one empty cell it returns 147,945 -- the default's answer, from the option named for missing data. `min_count=12` does return nothing known and only because this group has twelve rows: it would null every smaller group. The comparison is a per-group `sum(skipna=False)`, which is the rule itself and does not depend on the group size. Recorded because the next author will reach for min_count too, and because a check written against it would have reported a disagreement and called it a defect. What no check can verify is the protection that matters most here: sum is the only operation offered, because this step cannot tell a count from a rate and summing rates gives a number with no referent.

entries.criterion: every estimate and every interval bound within 1e-9 of statsmodels -- the risk ratio and odds ratio against contingency_tables.Table2x2 at riskratio_confint and oddsratio_confint, the risk difference against proportion.confint_proportions_2indep(compare='diff', method='wald') because Table2x2 CARRIES NO RISK DIFFERENCE, checked rather than assumed; the orientation asserted by recomputing both risks from the fixture's own cells, since a transposed table agrees on the odds ratio and disagrees on everything else; and every Epi Info label present WITH its source, naming the Epi Info AI results panel and never Epi Info itself -- a bare label or one claiming `epi-info` fails, because a field that can be filled unverifiably is worse than no field. Tighter than check 27's 1e-6 on purpose: that check found 1.9600 standing in for 1.959963984540054, and 1e-9 is what detects that class of defect rather than tolerating it.
notEstablished: Agreement with Epi Info. statsmodels is not Epi Info and this project makes no parity claim.
That the comparison is fair. The both-companies stratum, 16 of 32 sub-districts, is excluded by name and not controlled for -- Snow's own confounding, and the reason he went to the house level.
That the normal approximations are adequate. The Lambeth-only group has 18 deaths; an exact interval would be the better comparison there.
Which denominator is right. Houses and people give 8.40 and 5.35 over the same outbreak, and choosing between them is the practitioner's.
entries.measured: Twelve comparisons over two tables -- Snow's people from Tables VIII and XII, and his houses from Table IX -- every estimate, bound and method name exact, both orientations verified, the shared normal quantile equal to scipy's to 1e-12, and every Epi Info label present with `epi-info-ai-results-panel` as its source. People: risk ratio 5.351051 (3.355714 to 8.532834), odds ratio 5.373066, risk difference 0.004093. Houses: risk ratio 8.401853, odds ratio 8.642901, risk difference 0.027785.
entries.note: THIS CHECK CHANGED THE WIDGET'S DOCUMENTATION BEFORE IT SHIPPED, which is the strongest thing a lab check has done here. Fieldwork explained the 8.40-against-5.35 gap in the South London project as rate-versus-risk. The fixture refutes it: a risk ratio over the same houses is 8.401853429780243, the rate ratio's value BIT FOR BIT, because deaths per house is a risk when a house can hold at most one death and the two are the same division. Only the intervals differ, and only in the second decimal -- 6.8410 to 10.3189 from the Poisson form against 6.8450 to 10.3128 from Katz. So the gap is the DENOMINATOR and not the estimand, and the hazard is worse than first stated: a reader who takes 8.40 for the risk ratio beside the houses table is right, and is thereby taught that the substitution is safe, which holds only while the outcome is rare. Both tables are carried in one fixture because the comparison between them IS the finding. Agreement here says nothing about agreement with Epi Info, which this project does not claim. UPDATED 2026-10-26: the labels were read, on the practitioner's pointer that they "can be deduced from the results panel that Epi Info AI prints -- that's the closest I got to the real thing". Transcribed from the classic TABLES estimate table in epi-info-ai/wasm/demo/app.ts: Risk Ratio (RR), Odds Ratio (cross product) -- the qualifier kept, since the panel prints a conditional-MLE odds ratio beside it that is not computed here -- and Risk Difference (RD%), which that panel prints as a PERCENTAGE where this carries a proportion. So criterion 5 inverted: from 'the label must be null' to 'the label must be present and must name its source, and the source must not be Epi Info'. What it polices moved from the absence to the provenance, which is the same purpose.

entries.criterion: every part's value equal to a pandas left merge on the folded key, nulls included, with the two Streatham parts carrying one value between them and flagged shared; parts, rows, matched parts, matched rows, unmatched and shared counts all equal; 23 of 32 rows matching on UNFOLDED equality, which needs no normalisation to recompute and is therefore independent in the strongest sense available here; every folded key equal to its name with all non-alphanumerics deleted and no two distinct names folding together; and a part renamed to a place the table does not carry reported unmatched and named, with the other 32 unchanged.
notEstablished: That folding punctuation is the right rule for names. It is right for these two files, where every difference is a comma or a doubled space. A boundary spelling 'St Mary' against a table's 'Saint Mary' would fail this join, and whether failing is right there is a judgement about the data rather than an outcome of this check.

That the folding itself is correctly implemented. It is not independently reimplemented here, on purpose: a second copy written by the same author is not a second opinion. What is checked is a property it must satisfy -- that it changed nothing but non-alphanumerics and folded no two distinct names together.
That the 33 parts are the right geography. Streatham being two polygons is a fact about the digitisation. Both parts take the same rate, which is correct for a rate and would be wrong for a count.

That a sub-district rate measures an exposure. In the middle 16 sub-districts both companies supplied the same streets, so the rate there mixes two exposures -- Snow's own confounding, and why he went house to house.
entries.measured: Three cases over Snow's Table VIII through the declared rate. Folding punctuation: 33 of 33 parts and 32 of 32 rows matched, 2 shared, one duplicate-boundary-key diagnostic. Raw strings: 24 of 33 parts and 23 of 32 rows, with nine parts unmatched and named. Negative control: 'Camberwell Green' reported unmatched with an unmatched-boundary diagnostic naming it, the other 32 parts unchanged. The folding won 9 rows, 28 per cent of the table, every pair differing only in characters that are not letters or digits.
entries.note:
WHAT IS INDEPENDENT HERE IS NOT THE NORMALISATION, and the check says so rather than pretending otherwise. `normaliseName` is this project's own; a second copy written by the same author is not a second opinion, which is the trap check 27's record names. So three separable things are recomputed. The merge given keys is pandas' and fully independent. The raw-string baseline needs no normalisation at all. The folding is checked as a PROPERTY -- every folded key equals its name's alphanumeric reduction and no two distinct names fold together -- which is weaker than an independent fold and still refuses one that expanded St. to Saint, dropped a word, folded two names together or touched a letter.

AND THE DATA CANNOT SUPPLY A NEGATIVE CONTROL, which is the finding worth carrying. Snow's table and these boundaries have no pair differing by more than punctuation, so nothing in the example tests a name that OUGHT not to match -- 32 of 32 is also the score of a rule that matched too readily. One part is renamed to Camberwell Green, a real place the table does not carry. Jaro-Winkler to the name it replaced is 0.925 by rapidfuzz and 0.925 by jellyfish, so a similarity-based linkage at the usual 0.90 threshold would have ACCEPTED it. This widget has no threshold and no review band and reports the part unmatched; the two figures are what that decision is worth, and are reported rather than asserted, in the role the score interval plays in check 27.

notebookNote: `notebook` names the lab notebook that carries the check, and `diveDeeper` the heading of its Dive Deeper section where it has one -- the part written for a practitioner who wants to understand the widget rather than for a reviewer checking it (experiment 94). Both are recorded rather than derived from the check id: `24-project-forward` lives in `24-project-vs-pyproj.ipynb`, so matching on the leading number works by luck and would break the first time a check and its notebook are named differently. The application reads `diveDeeper` to decide which widgets offer the link, and scripts/validate-dive-deeper.mjs refuses a heading the notebook does not actually carry.
